Use the Bump tool to elevate or dig the terrain in the shape of a bump centered at the cursor.This is the simplest way to quickly modify the terrain.
Set the Speed parameter to control the speed of the modification of the terrain by the bump tool.

Use the Set to Height tool to uniformly modify the terrain to a desired height, either by setting a numeric height or taking the height from an existing terrain.
Set the Speed parameter to control the speed at which the terrain will flatten.

Use the Raise or Lower tool to increase or decrease the terrain with a fixed height increment that will remain constant as long as you keep painting.
Set the Height parameter to adjust height increment.

Use Smooth to soften out the terrain and even out irregularities.
Set the Speed parameter to control the speed at which the terrain will be smoothened out.

Use the Ramp tool to create a linear ramp between two positions.
The Ramp tool can be useful to make higher terrains accessible, as well as evening out the terrain below a road, for example.

Use the Erosion tool to give terrain shapes a more natural look by simulating land slides starting from the area of your cursor.
Set the Density parameter to control the speed at which erosion occurs.
Set the Deformation parameter to control how much the terrain will be affected by the operation.
Set the Landslide parameter to control the strength at which the erosion will be carving the terrain.

Use the Noise tool to break the smoothness of the terrain in random natural patterns.
The Noise tool can be very useful to create mountains, after which you can apply Erosion.
Set the Speed parameter to control the speed at which modification occurs.
Set the Roughness parameter to control the size of the random patterns. A high value creates many small bumps and a small value creates larger and smoother terrain.

Use the Add tool to place new objects in the map at the location of the cursor.
The directional buttons allows you to navigate through the different categories of objects.
You can also modify the object orientation before placing it by using the Rotate action.

Use the Edit Objects (2D) tool to access the basic operations to manipulate objects, such as making a selection of objects within a terrain area, moving them on the terrain surface, changing their orientation, and duplicating the selection.
The Radius parameter controls the size of the area in which you want to select the objects.
The Selection Type parameter allows you to either select only the object closest to the center of the cursor, or all objects contained within the area.

Use the Edit Objects (3D) tool to access advanced editing operations to manipulate objects, such as selecting objects with a cursor, placing objects at precise locations, as well as modifying the height and tilt of objects.
Set the Selection Type parameter to only select the object closest to the center of cursor, or select the biggest object in that area and all the objects in its neighborhood. For example, this can be useful for quickly selecting a house and all its content inside.
Set Movement Type parameter to move objects either linearly or by following the terrain's surface.

Use the Select Objects tool to define a precise selection that will stay locked until you cancel the selection. This can be useful for manipulating a complex set of objects without losing your selection. A red box indicates the locked state of the selection.
You can select multiple objects in a rectangular area by toggling the cursor, moving it to the top-left corner of the rectangle you wish to draw, holding the select action and then moving the cursor to the bottom-right corner. After releasing the select action, you will have selected all objects within that rectangle.
The selection process works in the same way as in the Edit Objects tool. Please refer to its section for more information.

Use the Snap tool to move one or more objects so they match correctly with another object.
The Snap tool works well with objects that naturally link together like fences, bridges or fort pieces.
This tool is different from the auto-snap mode which snaps objects together automatically when you move them near each other. This tool lets the user define precisely what should be snapped and with different settings.
The Snap Angle and Angle Direction parameters let you either specify an angle at which you want the objects to be linked at with a specific direction, or if objects should be snapped together without changing their current orientation.

Use the Collection Systems tool to quickly apply vegetation to an area of the map.
Assign a type of vegetation to an empty slot and then paint the chosen vegetation with the cursor.
You can also change the type of vegetation of a given slot at any time, allowing you to experiment with different themes.

Use the Paint Texture tool to give a different look to the terrain like grass, dirt or rock.
Assign a texture to an empty slot and then paint the chosen texture in your map.
You can also change the type of texture of a given slot at any time, allowing you to experiment with different looks.
Set the Minimum and Maximum Slope parameters to control the angle of the terrain slope, in degrees, on which the texture will be applied. This can be useful for only painting the sharp angles of a hill or mountain with rock.
Use the Environment Settings tool to set the time of day, clouds, weather ambiance, as well as the level of water in your map.

Use the Map Limits tool to define the boundaries of the playable area in the map.
Players who cross the map limits must return to battle before the countdown ends. Players who do not return to battle before the countdown ends will die.

Use the Road tool to draw a road path on the terrain. Control the points on the road to modify the path of the road.
Assign a road texture to an empty slot and then paint the road path in your map.
Set the Width parameter to adjust the width of the road.

Use the Snapshot tool to take a representative picture of your map. This snapshot will appear in the map browser so players looking for a new map to download will see it. So make sure you take a great picture of your map so players want to play it!

Use the Preview Final Map menu to view your map at the same quality that will be used while playing in multiplayer.
All terrain shadows will be fully generated, and rock textures will attempt to project correctly to avoid a stretched look.
In the Map Properties menu, set the map name, battlezone size and the number of players you recommend for the map.

Use the Validation tool to make sure all the rules of a game mode are respected in order to play your map in multiplayer.
Most of the time, this will consist of a required number of spawn points and other game objects such as transmission points, etc.
There are also more general rules that must be respected in every game mode, such as correctly placing spawn points and other game objects free of any collision with other objects, as well as respecting the given budgets.
You can quickly find an invalid object or the context of an error by simply selecting the error message.
Enable or disable the display of collection systems.
Enable or disable the display of fog.
Enable or disable the display of water.
Enable or disable the display of shadows.
Enable or disable the display of object helper icons.
When enabled, objects will keep their relative height to the terrain whenever the terrain is being modified.
Enable or disable the 3 indicators of budget at the top of the HUD.
When enabled, you will be prompted to confirm your deletion of an object to make sure it is not a mistake.
When enabled, objects that have specific anchor points defined, such as fences, bridges and fort pieces, will automatically link together when moved nearby each other.
When enabled, the auto snap will also adjust the object orientation to match the snapped object, or reset the tilt of an object when the angles are close to 0 degrees.
When enabled, the objects will automatically snap to the terrain when objects are slightly above or below it.
When enabled, the camera will not be able to go below terrain.
When enabled, the camera will not go through objects.
When enabled, the camera will make sure the cursor always stays within your view area when an operation occurs.

The Memory bar represents the variety of the resources used by the objects of your map. If you use many different types of objects that do not share common resources, then performance may suffer.
It is recommended to pick objects in related families to keep this indicator within limits. If the limit is exceeded, try deleting types of objects that are used only once or replacing them with objects that are used elsewhere.

The Objects bar represents the quantity of objects and collections you have used in your map. Not every object weighs the same, as you are able to see with the orange indicator that shows the cost of your current selection.
It is recommended to keep an eye on this meter to make sure your map stays within budget limit and performance guidelines. If the limit is exceeded, try removing objects or collections that have a high cost.

The Performance bar estimates how smooth the gameplay should be in the area you currently are in.
When the indicator is on GREEN, you get the smoothest experience. It is generally recommended to maintain this indicator in the green area wherever possible.
YELLOW indicates that the area could suffer from poor performance and should have less content to be optimal.
RED means you have exceeded the performance limit and this will result in poor or stuttering gameplay. You must remove content in order for the map to be playable.
When enabled, you will not take any damage or die when testing your map.

Use the Flatten tool to create a flat terrain surface from the starting point, often suitable for gameplay areas.
Set the Speed parameter to control the speed at which the terrain will be flattened out.
Use the Hole tool to completely remove sections of terrain. This can be used to then create caves and tunnels, by moving rocks or other appropriate objects in the hole to create an interior section.

Use the Water Layers tool to create a water plane of a given material within a sector of 64x64 meters. With careful usage of this tool, one can create a map with different water levels, also useful for placing waterfalls.
When enabled, you will be ignored by mercenaries, wildlife, and other characters when testing your map.
This feature requires enabling AI data generation in the map properties. Do you wish to enable?

The Lock Map Editing option prevents anyone from opening this map in the editor, except for its original creator. We strongly recommend you not to enable this option, as it prevents others from learning map techniques or making unexpected, great additions to one's map, all while keeping the original creator fully credited. But the option is there if you really want it.

The navigation mesh represents all the areas within with an AI-controlled character or vehicle can navigate in. Blue areas are used by characters, orange by ground vehicles, and purple by water vehicles.
Note that disjointed areas effectively mean that it will not be possible to cross between them, so it is extremely important to make sure all passages are appropriately connected. You can fix most issues by placing objects so they lie flat with each other.

The available covers, displayed as yellow rectangles on the map, represent all areas characters can use to take cover when engaging in a firefight.
It is important to have lots of them while covering as many angles as possible, to make sure AI characters are able to defend themselves against threats appropriately.
Make sure to add plenty of cover objects, such as walls, crates, trees, etc. to have a good density of covers in your gameplay areas.

Welcome to the Far Cry® 3 map editor!
{TX_PCButton_W}{TX_PCButton_A}{TX_PCButton_S}{TX_PCButton_D} Move around {TX_PCButton_Shift} Move faster {TX_PCButton_R_Mouse_Small} Rotate camera {TX_PCButton_MouseClick_Small} Pan camera {TX_PCButton_L_Ctrl} + {TX_PCButton_G} Test in-game
To start working, select a tool located in your toolbar.
To erase vegetation, hold the CTRL key and start painting.
To dig the terrain instead of raising it, hold the CTRL key and start painting.

Use the Add Object mode to place new objects in the map at the location of the cursor.
You can navigate through the different categories of objects by either using the drop down list, or by double-clicking on the folders. You can return to the parent folder at any time by pressing the "Go to parent" button.
You can also modify the object orientation before placing it by holding the CTRL key and the left mouse button to rotate that object.
By checking "Object preview mode", you can get a full-screen preview of the current object, allowing you to see every detail of the available assets.

To prevent selecting objects by mistake, you can use the "Freeze selection" button to make the objects in your current selection unselectable. If you want to modify such objects again, simply use the "Unfreeze all objects" button.

Use the Move Object mode to modify the position of the objects in your map.
Once you have selected one or more objects, click and hold the left mouse button on one of the arrows of the gizmo, in order to move the objects in the direction of the arrow you have selected.
You can also directly click on an object, and while holding the left mouse button, quickly move it at the position given by your cursor. While moving a selection in that way, you can also hold the CTRL key to quickly rotate the selection instead of moving it.
You can clone the content of your selection by holding the SHIFT key and moving the selection using either of the two ways described above. The previous content will stay where it was.
You can move a selection to a chosen location by pressing the ALT and SHIFT keys, then clicking where you want to place it.
You can move a selection by a fixed increment by checking "Use snap grid". Specify the increment by setting the "Snap grid size" parameter. "Snap with object size" will use increments that are the same as the object's bounding volume.
The "Drop selection" button will drop the objects until a physic interaction is found. This can be useful for making sure an object match either the ground or another object. If "Group selection" is activated, the objects relative height will be preserved, otherwise each object will be dropped individually.

Use the Rotate Object mode to modify the orientation of the objects in your map.
Once you have selected one or more objects, click and hold the left mouse button on one of the arrows of the gizmo, in order to rotate the objects around the direction of the arrow you have selected.
You can rotate a selection by a fixed increment by checking "Use snap angles". Specify the increment by setting the "Snap angle" parameter.
The "Reset tilt" button will make sure the bottom of the objects faces the ground directly.

To snap objects, click on the source reference object with the left mouse button, and while holding it, drag towards the target reference object, after which you can release the button. Small points will appear to indicate they will be used as reference for snapping the selection.

The "Group selection" checkbox allows you to determine whether you want to move your selection using one of its objects as a reference, or by treating the selection as a whole, where the reference is the center of the selection. A white box will surround your selection to indicate it is being treated as a group.

The "Neighborhood selection" checkbox will attempt to find the biggest object near your cursor and then select all the objects in its neighborhood automatically. For example, this can be useful for quickly selecting a house and all its content inside.

The "Axis type" parameter determines the orientation of the gizmo used for manipulating a selection. "Local" indicates the arrows will be oriented to match the orientation of its reference object. In that way, the arrows are in the direction of the object's own front, left, or up side. "World" indicates the arrows will always be in the same direction.

Use the "Select" mode to select a point by clicking on it. You can also select multiple objects by clicking and holding the left mouse button to define a rectangle of selection. When holding the SHIFT key, you can add points to your selection. When holding the CTRL key, you toggle the points to be either inside or outside of your selection.
While in "Select" mode, you can move selected points by clicking on one of them, and moving the mouse while holding its left button.
Use the "Draw" mode to let the editor add points automatically by following the movement of your mouse while holding its left button. Note that this feature only works when no points exist, or when the action is started on an end point.
Use the "Add" mode to add a point by clicking and holding the left mouse button, either from a endpoint or from a segment.
Use the "Remove" mode to remove a point under your mouse while holding its left button.

The performance indicator estimates how smooth the gameplay should be in the area you currently are in, by displaying the averaged number of frames per second the editor currently runs at.
Of course, this number may vary from one PC to another, so it is often a good idea to make sure the frame rate is consistently above 45 fps using a standard resolution and configuration across your map.

The object cost indicator counts the weight of all objects and collection systems used within your map, in order to give an idea of how much content there actually is.
While there is no imposed limit on this meter, it is recommended to stay within 40000-50000 to help most players having a good performance.

The memory usage indicator counts the memory size of all the unique resources, such as geometry and textures, used within your map. This in turn can have an impact on loading times and overall performance.
While there is no imposed limit on this meter, it is recommended to stay below 100 to help most players having a good performance.
The cursor position displays the 3D world coordinates of what's directly under the mouse cursor, whether it be terrain, water, or an object.
The camera position displays the 3D world coordinates of your current view point.
The camera speed indicates the speed at which your view point moves, in meters per second.

The goal of The Grid is to get one of the Data Keys into the Target Node using as few moves as possible.
To move a Data Key, fling it any of the four directions. The Data Key will keep moving until it hits a Firewall, another Data Key, or the edge of the grid.
Winning the game will give you a chance to earn encrypted data. Less moves gives you a better chance.
The Grid only has a certain amount of encrypted data available each day. If you want to maximize your daily rewards, try the harder difficulties to get better data!
Use hints if you get stuck. There's a limited number of hints available each day, so use them wisely.

Far Cry® 3 Outpost “Friends Matter”
Join your friends and get ahead in the game with the Far Cry® 3 mobile app for multiplayer and co-op. Earn advanced weapon mods for your favorite guns and customize your loadouts on the go! The next time you jump into a multiplayer match or co-op chapter, you’ll already be ready to play.
Features:
- Decode the encrypted data you find in-game to unlock advanced weapon mods and earn bonus XP. Don’t wait until you’re playing the game to start decoding. Instead, decode on the go! Once you unlock a weapon mod, you can accept it, give it to one of your friends or sell it for more XP straight from your phone.
- View and customize your loadouts so that you’re ready to play once you’re back in the game.
- Keep track of your progress through the Daily and Weekly Challenges. Completing these challenges will earn you XP.
- Check out your personal stats and the stats of your friends, including time played, level, top weapons, awards and more.
- Keep track of the maps you’ve made in the Map Editor. You can follow the current tier placements and how many people have liked or favorited your maps.
